coverage.method: Complete page-by-page extracted text read; rendered pages separately listed where inspected.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Irish rebellion: distinct allies and incompatible aims
findings.source_grounded_analysis: United Irishmen sought independence and organized through rural Defenders, whose grievances were more local and sectarian. French strategy needed proof of a rising while Irish leaders awaited intervention. Repression, arrests and uneven outbreaks preceded late French landings.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: United Irishmen; Defenders; Irish rebellion 1798; Wolfe Tone; French intervention
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not collapse urban national aspirations, peasant religion and French strategic aims into one programme.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Irish rebellion suppression and limits
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Wexford, Vinegar Hill, Humbert’s Mayo landing and Ballinamuck were separate episodes. Doyle emphasizes limited reach, inadequate French commitment and large death toll, while distinguishing comparison with Warsaw and French Terror.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Wexford; Vinegar Hill; Humbert; Ballinamuck; Wolfe Tone death
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep death-toll comparison denominators and the author’s argument about prospects; no automatic identity with the Vendée.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Batavian constitution: federalism, unitarism and French coups
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Initial Dutch sympathy and representative traditions mattered. Federalist-unitary stalemate, rejected 1797 draft, French-backed January purge and democratic 1798 constitution preceded attempted self-perpetuation and Daendels’s June coup, followed by regular elections.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Batavian Republic; federalism/unitarism; Dutch constitution; Daendels; French intervention
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish democratic constitutional provisions from coercive creation and subsequent operation; do not merge the two 1798 coups.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Costs and constrained choices of the Dutch alliance
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Occupation costs, British war and blockade, colonial loss, French tariffs and disrupted charity impoverished cities. Orange restoration and neutrality offered no easy alternatives; some domestic autonomy persisted despite French interference.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Dutch economy; blockade; poor relief; Church disestablishment; Orange; Anglo-Russian invasion 1799
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve both exploitation and the qualified account of political dependence; relief mechanisms need a route beyond war narrative.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Expansion of revolutionary France map
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Rendered whole page: map caption identifies territorial expansion, with visually distinct annexation, French occupation and sister-republic categories. Graph/map internals are excluded by policy, so this inspection does not generate subject evidence from internal labels.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: French expansion; map caption
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Ensure included caption treatment is not confused with excluded map internals; no inferential evidence from map symbols.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Belgium: exploitation, annexation and differentiated response
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Successive occupations treated Belgium as an extractive war resource; departmentalization and annexation ended extraordinary requisitions but introduced French laws. Rural hostility contrasts with urban accommodation and later industrial opportunity in the French market.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Belgium annexation; Agency for Trade and Extraction; Belgian departments; urban/rural responses
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep phases, policy changes and class/region differences. Urban pragmatism was not French national identity.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Belgian and Luxembourg revolts
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Clerical confiscation, oath refusal and conscription escalated into 1798 rural uprising. Rebels had local/religious aims and limited urban or elite support; French repression was more bloody. Passive resistance continued and recruitment remained low.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Belgian peasants’ revolt; Luxembourg uprising; Hasselt; conscription resistance; clergy deportation
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish decreed deportation from actual arrests and overt rebellion from continued passive evasion.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Rhineland annexation debate and incomplete assimilation
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Natural-frontier claims conflicted with peace strategy and German territorial interests. Hoche’s proposed Cis-Rhenan client state, Reubell’s annexation policy, provisional international consent and administrative departments had different statuses and dates.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Rhineland; natural frontiers; Cis-Rhenan Republic proposal; Reubell; Rastadt
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not make proposed client state an established republic, or departmental administration equal completed legal annexation.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Rhineland economy, religion and passive resistance
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Repeated occupation impoverished a front-line region. Customs severed Rhine commerce; flight of prince-bishops wrecked court-service economies. Feudal dues/tithes were retained for revenue before abolition; rental substitution diluted relief. Clerical resistance lacked a mass uprising amid dense troops and absence of conscription.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Rhineland requisitions; Rhine customs; court towns; tithe; German clergy; passive resistance
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve why comparable grievances yielded a different response than Belgium; liberty rhetoric is critically evaluated by Doyle.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Helvetic Republic: strategic access and imposed unity
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Italian conquests made Swiss Alpine passes strategically important. Ochs and La Harpe sought reform/emancipation, but local revolts pursued diverse older aims. France shifted from several states to one imposed constitution, coercing reluctant cantons.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Switzerland; Ochs; La Harpe; Vaud/Leman Republic; Helvetic constitution; Alpine passes
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish advocates’ intentions, local autonomy and French strategic purpose; retain constitution imposed without convention.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Swiss occupation, reform and democratic resistance
findings.source_grounded_analysis: City treasuries financed French armies and Egypt. Conscription demands met legislative refusal; rationalizing reform was unevenly received. Catholic valleys resisted both religion policy and loss of established democratic autonomy; wartime requisitions defeated promises of restraint.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Helvetic exploitation; Swiss militia; Catholic cantons; Valais; local democracy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not equate opposition to French centralization with opposition to all freedom or democracy.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Italian Jacobins and French priorities
findings.source_grounded_analysis: No general republicanization plan initially governed the invasion; Alba patriots were abandoned. Educated urban radicals hoped to revive Enlightenment reform after reaction, but French leaders suspected Year II politics and weak popular support, aiming first at strategic gains and extraction.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Italian Jacobins; Alba republic; Buonarroti; Enlightenment reform; Italian unification
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve source’s qualification that sister states emerged contingently, and diverse moderation/radicalism among patriots.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Italian exploitation and urban-rural resistance
findings.source_grounded_analysis: War contributions, requisitions, treasury and pawnshop seizures, art removal and generals’ profits funded armies and France. Pavia’s revolt and sack exemplify resistance; many dispersed rural revolts combined religious outrage and material loss.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Italy occupation; art plunder; military finance; Pavia; peasant uprisings
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Differentiate local resistance from unified nationalism; include civic welfare effects of pawnshop seizures.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Cispadane and Cisalpine formation
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Bonaparte encouraged limited cooperation while suppressing Milanese unity demands. Conservative Cispadane election results and strategic frontier problems helped produce Cisalpine consolidation. Venice became compensation for Austria; the new constitution and first officers were imposed.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Cispadane Republic; Cisalpine Republic; Milan clubs; Venetian settlement; Campo Formio
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Retain contingencies and distinctions of republic, constitution and territorial settlement; avoid claiming unification was France’s goal.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Cisalpine client rule and repeated coups
findings.source_grounded_analysis: France demanded troop maintenance, its own army and commercial preferences. Treaty resistance prompted a purge; later conflicts over radicalism, constitutional restriction and Brune’s disobedience caused repeated reversals. Jacobin refugees continued to seek Italian unity.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Cisalpine treaty; Cisalpine Fructidor; Brune; political purges; Italian unity
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Review direction and timing of each purge; conservative/moderate/radical replacements are not interchangeable.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Ligurian and Roman republics: different constitutions, common subordination
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Ligurian constitution was locally drafted and plebiscitary but financial refusal provoked a coup. Rome’s imposed institutions used antique labels while allowing French command to legislate; religious/economic changes undermined charity and popular support.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Ligurian Republic; Roman Republic; Roman Vespers; papal deportation; Roman poor relief
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve contrasting constitutional processes; antique terminology does not establish ancient institutional identity.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Parthenopean Republic and Sanfedist overthrow
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Championnet’s intervention exceeded Directory wishes and faced lazzaroni resistance. Retreat exposed Jacobins to Ruffo’s Holy Faith army; Ruffo mobilized social, rural-urban and religious grievances, even offering feudal relief before reformers. Subsequent reprisals were demanded over his opposition.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Parthenopean Republic; Championnet; lazzaroni; Ruffo; Sanfedists; Neapolitan repression
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not homogenize restoration forces, identify social protest exclusively with Jacobinism, or attribute court vengeance to Ruffo.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Piedmont and Tuscany: control and annexation
findings.source_grounded_analysis: French pressure displaced Piedmont’s king and annexation was rigged; Tuscany was occupied for wartime resources. Resistance drew on older anti-reform and subsistence grievances and included anti-Jewish attacks.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Piedmont annexation; Charles Emmanuel IV; Tuscany; Viva Maria; anti-Jewish violence
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve local historical causes and the source’s chronology inconsistency; do not treat all anti-French activity as rural.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Repudiation of French occupation and Italian Jacobin disillusion
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Peasants linked foreign soldiers, exactions, impiety and urban collaborators; some Jacobins also opposed French control. Langhe peasants carried Jacobin martyr images in an anti-annexation rising, complicating ideological labels.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Italian resistance; Jacobin disillusion; Langhe revolt; Marat/Le Peletier symbolism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Need meaningful distinctions beyond universal anti-revolution; political symbols and coalition alignments could cross expected boundaries.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Second Coalition victories and Bonaparte’s abandonment of Egypt
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Local opposition magnified coalition pressure. Stockach and Suvorov’s advances exposed overstretch and collapsed sister republics. Bonaparte learned late of European losses and left his army before receiving evacuation orders; eventual surrender followed.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Second Coalition; Stockach; Suvorov; collapse of sister republics; Egypt abandonment
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve chronology of information and orders; do not portray departure as compliance with an order he had received.

uncertainties.issue: Page366 prints February1798 for referendum after December1798 occupation; p367 describes impending annexation in February1799. Preserve internal chronology discrepancy and render if exact date is at issue.
